what_it_does: High-speed memory interfaces use PAM-4 signaling—a technique that encodes data by transmitting four different voltage levels instead of the traditional two (high/low), doubling the data rate in the same bandwidth. However, PAM-4's four levels are packed tightly together (only one-third the spacing of normal signaling), making the signal fragile and easy to corrupt by electrical noise. This paper describes a memory transmitter that uses a feed-forward equalizer (a circuit that pre-compensates the signal to counteract known channel distortions) and adds special encoding to reduce power consumption, enabling reliable 32–50 gigabits per second per pin on memory buses using single-ended (not differential) signals.
